title: A Single-Moding Approach to Teacher Productivity
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Adapting a CEO-versus-worker-bee idea from online entrepreneurs, Stuart proposes that teachers do their work in distinct modes: planning, prepping, teaching, reflecting and reviewing, and giving feedback. Each mode is either decision-making or execution, and trouble starts when we blend them, as when we break from unit planning to build a single prompt. Because teachers have little non-instructional time, they are tempted toward unconstrained hours and trivial tasks like constant email checking, which he frames as a matter of self-discipline and clear thinking. The practical habit is to catch yourself multi-moding and return to the mode you left. The post is a productivity and sustainability argument for the profession.
points: Teaching work divides into planning, prepping, teaching, reflecting and feedback modes that mix decision-making and execution.
Switching modes mid-task, such as creating a prompt in the middle of unit planning, is the signature of multi-moding and signals you should step back.
Scarce prep time drives teachers toward unconstrained hours and low-value tasks, making productivity a matter of discipline and clear thinking.
Feedback is singled out as the hardest mode to keep focused because it is time-consuming and tedious, so efficiency and limiting distractions matter.
quotes: It’s where we make decisions about curriculum, assessments, classroom management, objectives, and the direction of the class. The degree to which we get to make decisions on these things varies by school, but all of us have to do at least some work here. However, planning doesn’t do anything until it’s executed.

Teaching Mode: This is kind of a place where the Worker Bee and the CEO co-exist. We teach the lesson as planned and prepped, but we also make modifications based on checks for understanding and make note of how our plans might need to be adjusted.

Importantly, this is one of the hardest times to stay focused on being a Worker Bee because it’s usually both time-consuming and tedious. To make it less so, we need to make our feedback as efficient as possible and limit the degree to which we engage in distractions while doing it.

A key pressure point for teachers, of course, is that (at least in the USA) we’re given very little non-instructional time during the school day. Since these “prep periods” are so minimal, we find ourselves needing to do more in an hour than we can possibly do, and so we start talking ourselves into avenues of insanity like unconstrained working hours or treating relatively pointless tasks (e.g., frequent email-checking) as if they are important. This is a question not just of productivity but of productivity’s roots in self-discipline and clear thinking.

If we were planning a unit ten minutes ago and now find ourselves creating a mid-unit writing prompt, we are probably doing it wrong. Instead, we need to step away from the mid-unit Prep work and go back to Planning mode. Finish planning the unit — something like Wiggins’ Understanding by Design or Burke’s What’s the Big Idea helps here — and then become the worker bee who does the necessary prep work.

The longhand version is up to you; only you can decide how to use the time you have — the finite time, the time between when you’ve decided you’ll start working and when you’ve decided you’ll stop. You approach this like a tinker, like an experimenter, like someone who holds and tests hypotheses about how best to use time.
